That combination is why Burgenland can deliver reds with ripe black and red fruit while still tasting driven rather than thick.\n\nLeo Hillinger is a high-visibility modern Burgenland producer, and this bottling appears positioned as an accessible table red rather than a tightly delimited cru wine. Because the label is simply Burgenland, there is a limit to how precise anyone can be about site expression; the tradeoff is consistency and approachability. That extra heat pushes Blaufränkisch toward darker fruit and rounder tannin, while the grape’s naturally high acidity keeps the palate lifted. Across Burgenland, soils can include loam, limestone, schist, and iron-rich sites, but this wine’s broad appellation does not specify a narrower origin, so assigning one soil profile would be guesswork. Tannin is the drying, structural grip that comes from grape skins and seeds, and with Blaufränkisch you want it present because it frames the acidity and spice. parsed.hook: Burgenland Blaufränkisch works when the region’s warm Pannonian climate ripens the fruit without erasing the grape’s natural snap, and that is the lane this wine sits in. Under the broad Burgenland appellation rather than a single village site, it reads as a regional Blaufränkisch: dark cherry, plum, pepper, and enough acidity to keep 13% alcohol from feeling heavy.
parsed.wine_summary:
This matters less as a site-specific statement and more as a clear look at what Burgenland does well with Blaufränkisch. The appellation is broad and permissive, but Blaufränkisch is firmly one of its key red grapes, and the region gives it a very useful combination: warm growing conditions from the Pannonian plain and cooling influences that help the grape hold acidity. That combination is why Burgenland can deliver reds with ripe black and red fruit while still tasting driven rather than thick.

Leo Hillinger is a high-visibility modern Burgenland producer, and this bottling appears positioned as an accessible table red rather than a tightly delimited cru wine. Because the label is simply Burgenland, there is a limit to how precise anyone can be about site expression; the tradeoff is consistency and approachability. In the glass, expect the regional signature more than a single-parcel fingerprint: Blaufränkisch’s peppery edge, brisk acid line, and a fruit profile that leans from sour cherry toward blackberry depending on vintage warmth.
parsed.terroir_expression: Burgenland sits on Austria’s eastern edge under strong Pannonian influence, which means warmer, drier continental conditions than many Austrian regions. That extra heat pushes Blaufränkisch toward darker fruit and rounder tannin, while the grape’s naturally high acidity keeps the palate lifted. Across Burgenland, soils can include loam, limestone, schist, and iron-rich sites, but this wine’s broad appellation does not specify a narrower origin, so assigning one soil profile would be guesswork. What can be said directly is that regional Burgenland Blaufränkisch often tastes less severe than examples from cooler, rockier village sites and more centered on ripe cherry-plum fruit, black pepper, and a smooth but still fresh finish.
parsed.vinification_summary: Specific cellar details are not provided, so it is better to stay with what the style suggests. For a regional Burgenland Blaufränkisch at 13% ABV, the likely goal is clean fruit definition over extraction for its own sake: enough skin contact to pull color and tannin from Blaufränkisch, but not so much that the wine turns angular. Tannin is the drying, structural grip that comes from grape skins and seeds, and with Blaufränkisch you want it present because it frames the acidity and spice. If oak is used here, it is likely supportive rather than dominant, because heavy wood would blur the grape’s pepper-cherry profile that is the main reason to buy this style in the first place.
parsed.food_pairing:
Schnitzel with lingonberries — the wine’s acidity cuts the fried crust, and the tart fruit on the plate mirrors Blaufränkisch’s cherry edge.

Nashville hot chicken — peppery fruit and moderate body handle chili heat better than heavier, more alcoholic reds, while the acidity keeps the pairing from turning greasy.

Grilled lamb kofta with sumac yogurt — Blaufränkisch’s spice note links with cumin and char, and the yogurt cools the tannin.

Duck breast with sour cherry sauce — this is a direct regional-style match because the wine already leans toward cherry and plum, so the sauce extends the fruit instead of fighting it.

Venison loin with beet purée and juniper — for a fine-dining pairing, the wine has enough structure for game, and its bright line keeps earthy beet and juniper from reading too dense.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Moric Blaufränkisch Burgenland — same grape and region, usually with more tension and site precision.
Heinrich Blaufränkisch Leithaberg — comparable Austrian profile, often showing more mineral drive from limestone-heavy zones.
Wachter-Wiesler Blaufränkisch Eisenberg — similar grape with a cooler, more iron-toned, peppery expression.
parsed.style_profile: Medium-bodied dry red with bright acidity, firm-medium tannins, and peppery dark cherry fruit
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now if you want the fruit and spice in the foreground, especially for the older listed vintages. Store at a steady cool temperature and open the 2014 soon; broad-appellation Blaufränkisch can age, but this bottling is more about freshness and regional character than long cellaring.
parsed.value_assessment: $15-25 is the right expectation for a regional Burgenland Blaufränkisch from a visible producer. At that level it competes with Judith Beck Blaufränkisch and entry wines from Heinrich; it is worth buying if you want an Austrian red with real acidity and spice rather than another plush international red. The value is strongest for drinkers exploring Blaufränkisch without paying single-vineyard prices.
parsed.market_position: This belongs on by-the-glass restaurant lists, independent retail shelves, and Austrian-focused selections where staff want a food-friendly red that is not Pinot Noir and not Syrah. The audience is curious drinkers, sommeliers building versatile pairings, and regular buyers who like acid-driven reds with savory edges. Collectors chasing named sites will look elsewhere.
parsed.insider_take: Think of it as the anti-jam red in its price band. What people get wrong is expecting Blaufränkisch from warm Burgenland to behave like a soft, anonymous supermarket red; the point is the acid spine and peppery bite. Buy it for dinner, not for trophy-wine drama, and skip it if you only like reds that finish plush and sweet-fruited.
